title: C.E.L.L. Cross-Platform Game Engine
description: C.E.L.L. (Cross-Platform Emulation Library Layer) was a proprietary 2D game engine I designed to let the same game architecture run across Java- and C#-based platforms including Windows, Xbox 360, Windows Phone 7, Android, BlackBerry, OS X, Linux, and Java web deployment. The engine used a layered architecture consisting of native platform adapters, the MicroGen application/UI framework, the PlatformerLib gameplay layer, game-specific code, scripting, and an optional visual game editor. By 2012 it had already powered three released games, three 48-hour game jams, and roughly ten prototypes spanning platformers, RPGs, RTS games, space shooters, and puzzle games.

sections.title: Cross-Platform Architecture
paragraphs: C.E.L.L. was designed around the idea that Java and C# were similar enough to support a common engine architecture if platform APIs and language differences were isolated behind carefully designed interfaces.
The engine was primarily authored in Java 1.4-era syntax so the shared code stayed within a language subset that could be translated and reused across Java and C# targets.

sections.title: Four-Layer Engine
paragraphs: The engine was divided into four primary runtime layers, each building on the layer beneath it.

sections.title: Native C.E.L.L. Layer
paragraphs: The native layer was the portability boundary.
A platform-specific implementation exposed one common interface to the higher layers while wrapping each platform's graphics, sound, input, file, resource, collection, display, and utility APIs.

sections.title: Platform-Specific Native Wrappers
paragraphs: The same C.E.L.L. abstractions wrapped very different native APIs.
items: Java SE: AWT / Swing / BufferedImage / Graphics2D
BlackBerry: FullScreen / Bitmap / Graphics / media Player

sections.title: Unified Graphics API
paragraphs: C.E.L.L. normalized platform-specific graphics APIs into a shared drawing interface.

Game code could perform operations such as bitmap rendering, arbitrary rotation, text drawing, alpha blending, shapes, lines, and color changes without knowing which platform graphics API was underneath.

sections.title: Resource Management
paragraphs: The Resource Handler maintained a central cache for images and sounds so the same asset was not repeatedly loaded into memory.
Resources could be released in groups when changing ScreenPanels, helping manage the much tighter memory limits of mobile devices.

sections.title: Cross-Platform File & Save System
paragraphs: The native file layer hid differences between desktop file systems, web resources, Xbox project/external storage, and smart-device internal/external storage.
C.E.L.L. also implemented its own save-file mechanism by packing game/session values into a binary .SAV format rather than relying on incompatible native serialization systems.

sections.title: MicroGen
paragraphs: MicroGen was the second C.E.L.L. layer and acted as a small cross-platform application framework inspired by the basic ideas of Java Swing.
It provided enough reusable UI and navigation infrastructure to build complete menu-driven applications without using platform-specific UI code.

sections.title: ScreenPanel Architecture
paragraphs: Games were organized as interchangeable full-screen ScreenPanels for title screens, options, individual levels, win/lose screens, credits, and other application states.
Only one ScreenPanel was active at a time, and the Navigator and Session systems connected otherwise isolated screens.

sections.title: Cross-Platform Focus System
paragraphs: MicroGen included a focus system so UI screens could work across touch, mouse, keyboard, and controller-based devices.
The same menu could therefore be clicked with a mouse or touch screen and navigated with an Xbox controller.

sections.title: Animation System
paragraphs: MicroGen provided reusable named animations that could be played individually or chained into sequences.
Animation definitions were later incorporated into entity scripting and game behavior.

sections.title: Independent Game / AI Timing
paragraphs: The engine game loop could optionally separate rendering from game or AI calculations.
This allowed expensive simulation work to run at a lower update rate than the display frame rate.

sections.title: PlatformerLib
paragraphs: PlatformerLib was the layer where C.E.L.L. became a general-purpose 2D game engine.
Although named after platform games, its systems were designed broadly enough to support side scrollers, RPGs, RTS games, shooters, puzzles, and other genres.

sections.title: Physics
paragraphs: C.E.L.L. integrated the Box2D family at the PlatformerLib layer.
Java targets used JBox2D while Xbox and Windows Phone targets used Box2D.XNA.

sections.title: Multiple Collision Systems
paragraphs: PlatformerLib supported several collision approaches so each AI/entity implementation could use the technique appropriate to the game.

sections.title: Generic AI
paragraphs: Entities could have interchangeable intelligence components attached in code or script.
PlatformerLib included default behavior suitable for gravity-based side-scrollers and top-down RPG-style movement, while games could provide their own custom AI.

sections.title: Entity Architecture
paragraphs: Entities represented players, NPCs, interactive objects, and even scriptable background elements.
Entity definitions connected named animation, sound, and input capabilities to either AI or player-control logic.

sections.title: Layered Rendering
paragraphs: Game levels were composed from reusable rendering layers that could be stacked in arbitrary combinations.

sections.title: Camera System
paragraphs: C.E.L.L. supported multiple camera objects with one active camera.
Attaching the current camera to an entity allowed scrolling worlds to follow the player automatically.

sections.title: Sound Queue
paragraphs: The sound queue coordinated music and audio playback.
It could replay music, sequence short music clips into continuous soundtracks, or change musical sequences dynamically based on game state.

sections.title: Scripting System
paragraphs: C.E.L.L. moved level layout, entity creation, layers, input behavior, and event actions into external scripts where doing so improved portability and rapid development.
The scripting system intentionally complemented native Java/C# code rather than trying to replace it.

sections.title: Scripted Actions
paragraphs: Script commands could be grouped into batches and attached to triggers such as collision regions.

sections.title: Scriptable Game Screens
paragraphs: DefaultPlayScreen could construct complete game screens from scripts while custom ScreenPanels could still be hard-coded.
A single game could therefore freely mix scripted screens with specialized coded screens.

sections.title: Interchangeable Game Systems
paragraphs: ScreenPanels, AI, layers, and entities were intentionally reusable between games.
Game-specific components could be copied into another project and connected through configuration and scripts.

sections.title: Session & Navigation
paragraphs: A centralized Session object held play-session state while Navigator controlled screen transitions.
This separated individual screens from global state and simplified saving, loading, memory management, and screen reuse.

sections.title: Cross-Platform Input Commands
paragraphs: Game code did not consume raw platform input directly.
C.E.L.L. mapped keyboard, mouse, touch, gesture, controller, virtual controls, and scripted behavior into a shared command vocabulary.

sections.title: Input as Gameplay Commands
paragraphs: ScreenPanels, layers, AI systems, and entities registered for logical commands instead of physical buttons.
Scripts could issue the same commands as a player, making the input system useful for cutscenes, scripted movement, and AI-controlled sequences.

sections.title: Touch and Controller Abstraction
paragraphs: The command layer made it possible to map the same gameplay action to different physical controls.
For example, movement could come from a keyboard, Xbox D-pad or stick, Android touch button, swipe, virtual thumbstick, or script trigger.

sections.title: Resolution & Aspect Ratio Management
paragraphs: C.E.L.L. handled major differences in display resolution and aspect ratio between phones, tablets, desktops, and televisions.
The engine could render into a design-resolution buffer and scale while preserving aspect ratio, or use alternate-resolution asset sets while keeping game coordinates unchanged.

sections.title: Cross-Platform Fonts
paragraphs: The engine wrapped font behavior behind the native layer and generally favored broadly available system fonts or bitmap fonts.
XNA-specific font-resource requirements were handled inside the platform implementation.

sections.title: Portable Resource Naming
paragraphs: C.E.L.L. normalized differences in how platforms stored and named resources.
A logical path such as level1/init.script could be translated by the native platform layer into a flattened or indexed platform-specific representation without changing the game code.

sections.title: Java-to-C# Translator
paragraphs: I created a custom translator specifically for the C.E.L.L. codebase so Java engine and game code could be moved into XNA/C# projects with minimal manual work.

The translator recursively processed a Java project, scanned class and method hierarchies, converted .java files into .cs files, identified virtual/override methods, and translated the Java syntax patterns used by C.E.L.L.

sections.title: Java / C# Compatibility Rules
paragraphs: C.E.L.L. development deliberately avoided Java constructs that did not translate cleanly into C#.
Helper APIs and coding conventions were used so the Java source remained compatible with the eventual C# representation.
items: Avoidance of incompatible anonymous inner-class behavior

sections.title: Cross-Platform Targets
paragraphs: The 2012 engine article documents C.E.L.L. as supporting a wide range of Java- and C#-based deployment targets.

sections.title: Multiple Authoring Workflows
paragraphs: C.E.L.L. deliberately supported several ways to create a game.
items: Build through the C.E.L.L. Visual Game Editor
Mix code, scripting, and visual editing in the same project

sections.title: Visual Game Editor Integration
paragraphs: The optional visual editor generated and edited the same scripts used by the runtime.
The editor exposed layers, entities, AI, triggers, actions, collisions, and play testing to non-programmers while developers could still edit scripts or add custom code when needed.
The editor is documented separately in its dedicated portfolio card.

sections.title: Rapid Prototyping
paragraphs: The combination of reusable screens, layers, entities, AI, scripting, and visual editing made C.E.L.L. a rapid-prototyping environment.
In the 2012 article I described the editor as sometimes being capable of producing roughly 80% of a working game idea before custom programming was required.

sections.title: Proven Across Multiple Genres
paragraphs: By the time I documented C.E.L.L. publicly in 2012, it had already been used well beyond a single test project.

sections.title: Released Game Lineage
paragraphs: C.E.L.L. became the common technology behind multiple Square Particle releases and prototypes, including Santa's Route, Santa's Recession Bender, Flag Hunt, and the later Android-era Bridge Captain work.

sections.title: Published Engine Architecture
paragraphs: In 2012 I authored the Software Developer's Journal article "Designing a Cross Platform 2D Game Engine," a detailed technical walkthrough of C.E.L.L.

The article spans more than twenty pages and documents the engine layers, visual game editor and scripting, native-platform adapters, Java-to-C# translation, cross-platform input, resolution handling, fonts, and resource portability.

historicalNotes: C.E.L.L. expands to Cross-Platform Emulation Library Layer.
The original portfolio phrased the acronym as Cross Emulation Library Layer; Jamie's 2012 published article uses Cross-Platform Emulation Library Layer.
The 2012 Software Developer's Journal article is titled 'Designing a Cross Platform 2D Game Engine'.
The article begins on magazine page 53 and continues through page 74.
The published architecture identifies four primary runtime layers: Native C.E.L.L., MicroGen, PlatformerLib, and game-specific code.
The visual editor and scripting system interact with these runtime layers but are documented separately in the dedicated C.E.L.L. Visual Game Editor portfolio card.
C.E.L.L. was primarily authored using Java 1.4-era syntax as a lowest-common-denominator strategy.
The engine deliberately restricted use of Java-specific features to preserve C# compatibility.
Jamie created a custom Java-to-C# translator specialized for the C.E.L.L. codebase rather than a general-purpose language translator.
The translator recursively processed project trees, scanned class and method hierarchies, generated .cs files, handled virtual/override behavior, and translated known syntax differences.
By the time of the 2012 article, C.E.L.L. had been used for three released games, three 48-hour game jams, and roughly ten prototypes.
The article explicitly lists Windows, Xbox, WP7, Web/JNLP/Applet, OS X, Linux, Android, and BlackBerry as supported targets.
iOS was discussed as a possible future target through MonoTouch, not as an established C.E.L.L. platform.
Native C.E.L.L. abstracted events, graphics, resources, sound, collections, files, display/window behavior, bitmap handling, and utility/math behavior.
MicroGen provided ScreenPanels, ScreenComponents, focus handling, animation, common algorithms, a game thread, and screen navigation.
PlatformerLib provided physics, generic AI, collision handling, script parsing, cameras, input, sound queues, entities, generic layers, and DefaultPlayScreen.
C.E.L.L. used JBox2D on Java targets and Box2D.XNA on XNA targets.
Collision approaches included Box2D, pixel masks, tile masks, and rectangle intersection.
C.E.L.L. used logical input commands rather than directly exposing platform input to game code.
Scripts could issue the same input commands used by players.
C.E.L.L. supported resolution scaling, aspect-ratio preservation, alternate-resolution asset sets, font abstraction, and platform-normalized resource naming.
The article documents custom binary .SAV serialization to avoid incompatible platform-specific serialization.
The article describes the GUI editor as sometimes producing roughly 80% of a working game idea before custom code was needed.
The exact C.E.L.L. start/end dates are reconstructed from project chronology rather than stated as one explicit range in the article.
